name: Tea tree oil body wash

lead: Tea tree oil body wash is used by people aiming for fresher-smelling, clearer body skin, including for body odor and body acne. It contains an essential oil distilled from Melaleuca alternifolia leaves.

Its main component, terpinen-4-ol, shows antibacterial and antifungal activity in laboratory studies, and the idea is that fewer odor and acne bacteria means a cleaner smell and fewer blemishes. Clinical evidence is limited; a small early trial compared a 5% tea tree oil body wash with 4% nasal ointment to standard MRSA decolonization and found a nonsignificant trend favoring tea tree oil.

paras: People use it in place of regular body wash in the shower, often focusing on the back, chest and underarms, and keep it up as part of a routine. Many pair it with a moisturizer since cleansers can dry skin.
Skin irritation and allergic contact dermatitis are reported, and possible endocrine concerns in boys and men have been raised. Tea tree oil is toxic if swallowed.

web.title: Europe PMC search: tea tree oil acne

angle.text: Tea tree oil wash is used as a natural antibacterial cleanser to cut odor and acne bacteria, leaving body skin fresher and clearer. Lab studies show antibacterial activity; trials for odor or appearance are absent.

lead: Tea tree oil body wash is a cleanser containing tea tree (melaleuca) oil, an essential oil distilled from the leaves of Melaleuca alternifolia, a plant native to Queensland and New South Wales in Australia. [1] People use it as a natural antibacterial wash for the chest, back and shoulders, mainly to help keep body acne ("bacne") and odor-causing bacteria in check so the skin looks clearer. [2][3]

Tea tree oil is promoted for acne, dandruff, insect bites and fungal or bacterial skin infections. [1] A 2015 Cochrane review of acne therapies found one low-quality trial showing benefit over placebo, and a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of seven studies (445 patients) reported lower acne severity with tea tree oil than with controls, with mostly mild local adverse events. [1][4]

A small trial in 2000 compared a 5% tea tree oil body wash with 4% nasal ointment against standard MRSA decolonisation and found a trend, not statistically significant, favouring tea tree oil. [5] Reported adverse effects include skin irritation and allergic contact dermatitis, and the oil is toxic if swallowed. [1]
infobox: Began in the 1920s, led by chemist Arthur Penfold [1]
5% body wash in a 2000 MRSA study [5]
Approved complementary medicine in Australia; not an approved drug in the US [1]

paras: The oil is promoted for dandruff, acne, lice, insect bites, scabies and skin fungal or bacterial infections; Wikipedia says some claims have supporting evidence but few studies exist. [1] The European Medicines Agency recognises traditional use for minor wounds, insect bites and small boils. [1]

On T Nation, posters recommend washing bacne with diluted tea tree oil or a tea tree body wash, one calling it better than medicated acne products they had tried. [3] Another poster who started a tea tree body wash said they had heard it can make skin worse before better. [6]

In a T Nation thread on staph infections in jiu-jitsu, a poster says many people in the sport use tea tree oil. [2] The 2000 MRSA decolonisation trial combined a tea tree body wash with nasal ointment against a standard regimen. [5]

A 2015 Cochrane review of acne therapies found one low-quality trial showing benefit over placebo. [1] The 2026 meta-analysis found a pooled odds ratio of 0.74 for reduced acne severity versus controls in seven studies, with the authors calling for larger, high-quality trials. [4] A 2025 review of essential oils in skin care covering 70 studies reported tea tree oil as particularly effective for acne, and reviews of cosmeceuticals for acne note more human trial evidence for retinol, benzoyl peroxide and azelaic acid. [4]

Tea tree oil can cause irritation and allergic contact dermatitis, with risk rising as the oil oxidises. [1] It is highly toxic if swallowed and is a common cause of essential-oil poisoning in children in Australia. [1]

A possible link to breast enlargement in men and prepubertal children has been reported, and a 2018 National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences study identified four constituents as endocrine disruptors. [1] A 2007 Associated Press report, quoted on T Nation, said lavender and tea tree oils in some shampoos, soaps and lotions could temporarily leave boys with enlarged breasts. [7]
Commercial production began in the 1920s, led by chemist Arthur Penfold, who found the oil had antiseptic properties; plantations expanded in the 1970s and 1980s, mainly in New South Wales. [1]

A 2000 randomised trial compared a tea tree oil nasal ointment and 5% body wash with mupirocin and triclosan for MRSA carriage; the tea tree combination appeared to perform better but the difference was not statistically significant. [5] A 2026 systematic review of tea tree oil for acne included seven studies with 445 patients. [4] No studies specific to tea tree body wash for body acne or odor were found.

lore.intro: On T Nation, tea tree oil washes come up for back acne and for skin hygiene in contact sports, and occasionally in discussion of hormone-related side effects. [2][3][7]
